ai.literal: The goodness of companionship prosperity will give; the goodness of action desired all things will give.
ai.translation: The goodness of one's companions brings prosperity, but the goodness of one's own actions will yield everything that is desired.
ai.modern: நல்ல துணையின் நன்மை செல்வத்தைத் தரும்; செய்யும் செயலின் நன்மையோ விரும்பிய எல்லாவற்றையும் தரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the benefits of external support with the power of personal action. While having good associates and helpers (துணைநலம்) brings wealth and growth (ஆக்கம்), it is the purity and excellence of one's own actions (வினைநலம்) that delivers every single desired goal (வேண்டிய எல்லாம்). The poetic lengthening in 'தரூஉம்' emphasizes the steady flow of wealth from good company, but the poet shows that pure action is far superior because its rewards are limitless. Ultimately, personal integrity in what we do is the ultimate key to fulfilling all our aspirations.

ai.literal: Always shunning is necessary, along with fame, goodness not-yielding action.
ai.translation: One must always avoid those actions that do not yield both virtue and fame.
ai.modern: புகழையும் நன்மையையும் தராத செயல்களை எக்காலத்திலும் தவிர்த்தல் வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet outlines the criteria for pure action. A person must completely avoid any action that fails to bring both moral goodness (virtue) and public esteem (fame). The word 'nanri' refers to the spiritual or moral benefit of an action, while 'pukazh' refers to the honorable reputation it earns in society. If an action does not produce these two positive outcomes, it is deemed unworthy and must be shunned at all times.

ai.literal: Avoiding is necessary, fame-dimming actions, by those who say 'we will prosper'.
ai.translation: Those who say, 'We will prosper,' must avoid doing actions that dim their fame.
ai.modern: மேம்பாடு அடைவோம் என்று நினைப்பவர்கள், தங்களுடைய புகழைக் கெடுக்கும் செயல்களைச் செய்வதைத் தவிர்க்க வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet outlines the path of purity in action for those who aspire to rise in life. The word 'ஆஅதும்' refers to those who wish to grow, succeed, or prosper. The poet advises that such ambitious individuals must absolutely avoid ('ஓஒதல் வேண்டும்') any deed ('செய்வினை') that would diminish or ruin ('மாழ்கும்') their personal honor and fame ('ஒளி'). True prosperity cannot be built on actions that bring disgrace.

ai.literal: Even if distress befalls, disgraceful deeds they will not do, those who have a vision free from wavering.
ai.translation: Even when beset by severe distress, those who possess unwavering clarity of vision will not commit deeds that bring disgrace.
ai.modern: துன்பம் வந்தாலும், நடுக்கமில்லாத தெளிவான அறிவுடையவர்கள் இழிவான செயல்களைச் செய்யமாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the strength of character required to maintain purity of action during times of adversity. The key phrase 'நடுக்கற்ற காட்சி' refers to an unwavering clarity of vision or intellect that does not shake under pressure. People with such steady wisdom understand that temporary suffering is preferable to permanent dishonor. Therefore, even when faced with extreme distress, they refuse to perform disgraceful actions to ease their burden.

ai.literal: 'Alas!' saying, things that cause regret, do not do; if one does, then, such things not doing again is good.
ai.translation: Do not perform deeds that will make you cry out in regret, 'Alas, what have I done!' If you happen to commit such a mistake, it is best never to repeat it again.
ai.modern: 'ஐயோ! என்ன காரியம் செய்தேன்!' என்று வருந்தக்கூடிய செயல்களைச் செய்யக்கூடாது. ஒருவேளை அப்படிச் செய்துவிட்டால், மீண்டும் அத்தகைய செயல்களைச் செய்யாமல் இருப்பது நல்லது.
ai.explanation: This couplet from the chapter on Purity of Action advises against performing deeds that lead to remorse. The word 'eṟṟu' is an exclamation of grief or regret, used when one realizes a mistake. The poet warns that one should not do things that cause such regret ('iraṅkuva'). However, if a person does commit such an act ('ceyvāṉēl'), the best course of action is to ensure they never repeat ('ceyyāmai') such deeds ('aṉṉa') again ('maṟṟu').

ai.literal: Even if one sees the hunger of the mother who gave birth, do not do actions that the noble will condemn.
ai.translation: Even if one has to watch one's own mother suffer from hunger, one must not perform deeds that are condemned by the wise and virtuous.
ai.modern: தன்னைப் பெற்ற தாயின் பசியைக் காண நேர்ந்தாலும், சான்றோர்கள் பழிக்கும் தீய செயல்களைச் செய்யக் கூடாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the absolute purity of action under any circumstance. Even the most extreme and emotionally compelling situation, such as seeing one's own mother starve, does not justify committing an immoral act. The poet uses the word 'ஈன்றாள்' (she who gave birth) to evoke the deepest sense of duty and love, yet places the standard of 'சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை' (actions condemned by the noble) as an absolute boundary that must never be crossed. Thus, the purity of the means is held to be supreme, surpassing even the duty of saving a parent's life through wrongful deeds.

ai.literal: Blame having borne attained wealth-than, noble people's extreme poverty indeed foremost.
ai.translation: To the noble, extreme poverty is far better than wealth acquired by bearing blame and disgrace.
ai.modern: பழியை ஏற்றுக்கொண்டு அடைந்த செல்வத்தை விட, சான்றோர்களுக்கு மிகக் கடுமையான வறுமையே மேலானது ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the importance of maintaining purity of action. It states that for virtuous and noble people (சான்றோர்), living in extreme poverty (கழிநல்குரவு) is far superior (தலை) to acquiring wealth (ஆக்கம்) through shameful or disgraceful deeds (பழிமலைந்து). The word 'மலைந்து' means bearing or taking upon oneself, indicating that one should not accept blame just to gain material wealth. True nobility values honor and ethical conduct over ill-gotten riches.

ai.literal: To those who perform deeds, not shunning and rejecting forbidden deeds, those deeds themselves, even if they succeed, will bring distress.
ai.translation: To those who perform actions without shunning what has been forbidden, those very deeds, even if successfully completed, will only bring ruin.
ai.modern: விலக்கப்பட்ட செயல்களை விலக்கித் தவிர்க்காமல் செய்தவர்களுக்கு, அச்செயல்கள் வெற்றிகரமாக முடிந்தாலும் துன்பத்தையே தரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the importance of maintaining purity of action by avoiding forbidden deeds. The repetition of the root 'kaṭi' in 'kaṭinta' and 'kaṭintu' underscores the absolute necessity of shunning unethical actions. The poet warns that even if such forbidden acts are successfully completed and seem to yield results, they will ultimately bring only misery ('pīḻai') to the doer. True success cannot be built on a foundation of forbidden deeds, as the consequences of the action itself will eventually lead to ruin.

ai.literal: All things acquired making others weep will depart making the owner weep; even if lost, things of a good nature will yield benefits later.
ai.translation: Everything acquired by causing others to weep will depart causing tears; but righteous gains, even if they are lost at first, will yield good fruits in the end.
ai.modern: பிறர் அழும்படி துன்புறுத்திப் பெற்ற செல்வங்கள் எல்லாம் தாம் அழும்படியாக நம்மை விட்டுப் போய்விடும்; ஆனால், நல்ல வழியில் வந்தவை இழக்கப்பட்டாலும் பின்னர் நன்மையைத் தரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts wealth acquired through unethical means with wealth acquired through righteous means. The poet states that wealth gained by causing distress and tears to others will eventually vanish, bringing tears to the one who gathered it. Conversely, wealth earned through righteous deeds might be lost initially, but it will eventually yield beneficial results in the future. The repetition of the word 'அழ' (weeping) emphasizes the poetic justice of karmic retribution, where the pain inflicted on others returns to the perpetrator.

ai.literal: By deceit wealth having acquired, securing [it] is like having poured water inside an unbaked clay vessel and keeping [it].
ai.translation: Acquiring wealth through deceitful means and trying to secure it is like trying to store water in a vessel of unbaked clay.
ai.modern: வஞ்சக வழியால் செல்வத்தைச் சேர்த்து அதைப் பாதுகாக்க நினைப்பது, சுடப்படாத பச்சை மண் பாத்திரத்தில் நீரை ஊற்றி வைக்க முயற்சிப்பது போன்றதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against using dishonest means to acquire wealth. The word 'சலம்' here refers to deceit or dishonesty, which compromises the purity of action. Trying to protect or secure ('ஏமார்த்தல்') such ill-gotten gains is compared to pouring water into a pot made of unbaked clay ('பசுமண் கலம்'). Just as the raw clay pot will dissolve and lose the water, dishonest wealth will quickly disintegrate, destroying itself and its owner.
